summary: A report from an Internet Architecture Board workshop held in March 2006 that brought together network operators, standards people, and researchers. They discussed unwanted traffic such as DDoS attacks, spam, and phishing, where it comes from, and how well existing defenses work. The report also lists engineering and research topics that might help fight it. It is informational, not a specification.

subtitle: What operators, vendors and researchers told the IAB about spam, DDoS and the money behind unwanted traffic.

tldr.problem: Operators, standards people and researchers were working on unwanted traffic in separate circles, with no shared picture of where it came from, how bad it was, or which countermeasures actually worked.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB held a two-day workshop in March 2006 and gathered reports from operators of backbone networks, access networks, enterprises and DNS services, then summarized the vulnerabilities, the existing tools, the tools in the pipeline and the open research questions.
tldr.outcome: The report concludes that the root cause is an underground economy that pays for the traffic, and that the Internet has no effective deterrent because nobody is responsible, nothing can be traced back, and the law has not caught up. It lists immediate steps for the IETF, the IAB and the IRTF.

sections.title: The Workshop and Its Goals
sections.content:
This RFC reports the outcome of a workshop the Internet Architecture Board held on unwanted Internet traffic, on March 9 and 10, 2006 at USC/ISI in Marina del Rey, California. Experts from the operator, vendor and research communities were brought together to share what they were seeing, and the primary goal was to foster interchange between those three communities about unwanted traffic as seen in distributed denial-of-service attacks, spam and phishing.

The goals were to understand the ultimate sources of the unwanted traffic, to assess its impact and the effectiveness of existing solutions, and to identify engineering and research topics that the IAB, the IETF, the IRTF and the wider research community could take up to build effective countermeasures. The workshop succeeded in identifying the major sources of the unwanted traffic and in making a critical assessment of the existing mitigation tools. Time ran out, so for some important issues only the surface was touched, and because the primary focus was collecting and sharing the state of affairs, deriving solutions is left as the next step, to be done in part as activities within the IAB, the IETF and the IRTF.

The report is a summary of the participants' contributions and is not an IAB document, so the views it records do not necessarily reflect IAB views. Some product and company names appear, but a mention of any product should not be read as an endorsement of it, since there may well be equally relevant alternatives in the market.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the write-up of a two-day meeting where the people who run networks, the people who build tools and the people who study them talked about the traffic nobody wants: denial-of-service floods, spam and phishing. The main finding is that this traffic is bought and sold, and that the Internet has no way to trace it or punish it.

sections.title: The Underground Economy
sections.content:
The first message the workshop brings to the Internet community is the existence of an underground economy, which supplies an enormous amount of monetary fuel that drives the generation of unwanted traffic. The incentive feeds on an Internet that is to a large extent wide open: open in the sense that it fosters innovation but offers virtually no defence against abuse, and connects to millions of mostly unprotected hosts owned by millions of mostly naive users. The Internet was also designed without built-in auditing trails, which was appropriate at the time but makes malicious activity hard to trace, and the legal system has yet to adapt to regulating cyberspace. Together these mean there is no effective deterrent.

The underground economy grew from a barter system into a giant shopping mall that commonly runs on IRC servers. These servers provide online stores selling information about stolen credit cards and bank accounts, malware, bot code, botnets and root access to compromised hosts and web servers, along with DDoS attack stores and stores selling access to compromised routers. The miscreants are generally not skilled programmers, but with money they can hire professional writers to produce well-phrased spam and coders to build new viruses, worms, spyware and botnet control packages. Stolen goods are turned into cash through remailers, online marketplaces, money launderers and cashier's cheques, with the destination bank accounts closed as soon as the money is withdrawn.

The botnets moved on. In the early days their activity was largely devoted to DDoS attacks and was relatively easy to detect; as the economy evolved they went from easily detectable behaviour to masquerading as normal user network activity, which makes detection very difficult even for vigilant system administrators. The driver is a change of intent. Early attacks were largely anarchic, done by script kiddies to disrupt systems or to show off, while today the activity is mostly ordinary crime: systems are quietly subverted for future financial gain rather than visible disruption.

Compromised systems are the major source of the problem. Most end hosts run vulnerable platforms, and users arrive in the online world without the training to understand the implications. Viruses and worms exploit bugs in operating systems and applications, sometimes even in anti-virus programs, phishing sites install malware, and viruses now also spread through peer-to-peer file sharing, so infected machines include home PCs, corporate servers and even government firewalls. All platforms are vulnerable, not only Windows, and routers are not exempt, with a high-end router making a much more effective DoS launchpad than a bundle of home PCs. Quietly subverting large numbers of hosts while leaving their normal function and connectivity largely unimpaired is now a major aim, and it appears the miscreants are all too successful at it: bots are hard to detect and the owners usually do not know. Even after being notified, some owners do not fix the problem as long as their own interest, such as playing online games, is unaffected, so a large botnet can be assembled from multi-millions of compromised hosts, each sending an insignificant amount of traffic but together exceeding the capacity of the best engineered systems.
sections.plainLanguage: The traffic is not made by hobbyists any more. There are shops, most of them on chat servers, that sell stolen card details, malware and access to machines that have been taken over. The people running them hire writers and programmers to produce spam and viruses, and they quietly take over large numbers of ordinary computers without their owners noticing.

sections.title: How Bad Is the Problem for Each Kind of Operator
sections.content:
The impact differs by the kind of operator. For backbone providers, whose business is packet forwarding, the measure of the problem is whether DDoS traffic affects network availability; spam and malware are not a major concern because backbone networks do not directly support end users. In the majority of attacks the traffic can originate from almost anywhere, and regions with high-speed user connectivity but poorly managed end hosts are often the source, because miscreants look for targets offering maximal returns with minimal effort. Backbone networks are well provisioned, so core routers and backbone link capacity are not much affected by most attacks: a 5Gbps attack could be absorbed easily. DDoS attacks do saturate access networks, though, and multihomed customers with several well-provisioned connections can suffer from the aggregated traffic arriving from all directions.

For access providers, the most severe impact is not bandwidth exhaustion but the customer support load it creates. They are effectively the help desk for many customers, especially residential ones: during the Microsoft Blaster worm attack the average time taken to handle a customer call was over an hour, and because help desks are expensive to staff, a single call can cost the provider the profit of the whole customer relationship. Most providers therefore offer free security software, which many customers never install or cannot configure correctly. Past experience suggests that notification has little impact on repair behaviour, that there is no significant difference between industries or between business and home users, and that patching follows an exponential decay with a time constant of approximately 40 percent per month, so about 40 percent of computers are patched quickly and about 40 percent of the remaining vulnerable computers in each following month show signs of being patched, leaving a few percent unpatched after six months. Unmanaged computers are often replaced rather than repaired, and the infection happens during the installation of the replacement.

For enterprise networks, the operators are more willing to investigate breaches but hesitate to pay a high price for protection, and false positives are costly, so they prefer false negatives to false positives and generally prefer prevention to detection. They sort deliberately created unwanted traffic into three categories. "Nuisance" covers spam and peer-to-peer file sharing, which operators worry about as a significant share of the total network load, as a channel for malware propagation, and as a copyright risk. "Malicious" is the traffic that spreads malware: small in volume but costly in damage, and the clean-up requires highly skilled operators. "Unknown" is traffic whose purpose and sources nobody knows; it can be obscured by encryption or encapsulation, or covered up as legitimate traffic, and the existing detection tools are ineffective against it, so a stealth worm can open a backdoor and stay dormant. For DNS operators, the problem appears as increasingly significant DDoS attacks on the .com, .net and root servers, including reflection attacks using spoofed source addresses, causing bandwidth and resource exhaustion and disrupting critical services. The only effective and viable mitigation reported is over-engineering: more link bandwidth, more servers, more processing power and network anycast.
sections.plainLanguage: Who is hit depends on where you sit. Backbone providers can absorb most floods because their pipes are big; access providers are buried in help-desk calls; enterprises worry about volume, damage and unknown traffic; and DNS operators can only buy more capacity.

sections.title: Vulnerabilities, Existing Solutions and Their Shortfalls
sections.content:
The workshop first collected the major vulnerabilities. Packet source address spoofing is used mostly for reflection attacks, and while the spread of botnets means not every attack needs a spoofed address, many still do. BGP route hijacking is listed with source address spoofing as one of the two most critical vulnerabilities on the Internet in an Arbor Networks survey, and miscreants have been observed hijacking bogon prefixes to inject spam messages, which does not affect normal packet delivery and so is rarely noticed. Port scan attacks look for open TCP or UDP ports, and the reaction of closing unused ports has pushed application designers towards carrying everything over HTTP, which does not block attacks but moves the vulnerability elsewhere. A TTL that changed without a matching change in routing used to suggest subverted traffic, but mobile hosts roaming inside an operator's network change the path, so the TTL no longer means anything. Network authentication as used today is far too complex for users to apply and hard to make work with new wireless access technologies, where the underlying data link layer can change during a single session. And many useful security tools are simply not used extensively.

The solutions in use are modest. For backbone providers, adequate provisioning reduces the effect of DDoS on the backbone, and the answer that received most mentions was BCP 38, ingress filtering (RFC 2827), which can effectively block attacks using spoofed source addresses, with BCP 84 (RFC 3704) extending it to multihomed networks. Access Control Lists and BGP null routing are the two tools most commonly used to mitigate DDoS, and they are effective, especially at or near the victim's site, but they rely on manual configuration, they block legitimate packets along with the attack traffic, and an overly long ACL list can significantly slow packet forwarding in a router. Unicast reverse path filtering implements a restricted form of BCP 38 without the effort of maintaining ACLs, using the routing table to check that a valid path back to the source exists, but because asymmetric routing is prevalent the strict test may have to give way to the loose one, and the loose test is no guarantee against all cases of spoofing, so an ACL may still be needed for exceptions.

Enterprises have more tools. Firewalls are the most widely deployed, but their effectiveness against protecting confidential information is weakened by spyware installed internally and they are ineffective against attacks from inside the perimeter. Application level gateways are becoming more widely used, but they need application-specific support and often cache all in-flight documents, so configuration is difficult and costs are high, which is why operators prefer network level protection. Anti-spam measures consume significant human resources, and the newer learning filters may reduce both false positives and false negatives. Computer admission control, where a computer gets network access only if it belongs to a valid user and appears to have the most recent patches, is a more recent and more expensive development.

The shortfalls fall into three kinds. The tools are inadequate: operators largely rely on their own experience and skills with time-consuming manual operations. The deployments are inadequate: the known measures are not widely deployed because they cost resources that may not be available, because the operational community is not educated about the importance of patching and upgrades, and because a solution must be designed with the right incentives to promote deployment; effective protection also needs coordination between competing providers, and it is often hard even to find contact information for the operators of other networks. The education is inadequate: easily guessed passwords and plaintext password transmission are still common, and the ultimate solution to the compromised-host problem is a well-informed, vigilant user community. One position raised was that protecting the Internet might require replacing unconstrained open access with strictly controlled access, but the rough consensus was that enforcing controlled access is not the best solution. Three needs were identified instead: a commonly agreed bar for security assurance so that service providers can do risk assessment, traceability to allow tracking of abnormal behaviour, and liability for someone who fails to follow recommended practices.
sections.plainLanguage: The tools exist but they are crude and barely used. Filtering of forged addresses would block a lot of attacks, yet almost nobody deploys it, because it costs money and brings no direct benefit to the site that pays for it. The report says the gap is as much about incentives and education as about technology.

sections.title: Solutions in the Pipeline and the Wishes
sections.content:
Several solutions were being worked on. A central policy repository would hold policies known to work properly, such as which neighbour router or autonomous system is doing proper ingress filtering, and the configurations operators use to upgrade their routers. As a shared resource it would need validation and authentication so that it does not become the cause of vulnerabilities, and it would only be viable if the savings for individual operators exceeded the cost of running it.

Flow-based tools are widely used to extract information from the network and data link layers, and they can find the sources of almost any type of traffic, including unwanted traffic. They make DDoS traceback, traffic and peering analysis, and detection of botnets, worms and spyware possible. They monitor flows and build a baseline of what normal behaviour looks like, so that anomalies can be spotted and judged, and the approach can be taken further by identifying signatures for particular types of traffic. The report compares this to sonar: once a particular submarine is identified, its signature can be recorded so the same one can be recognised quickly later. Examples named are Cisco IOS NetFlow, sFlow and NeTraMet, the last based on the IETF RTFM and IPFIX standards.

The Internet Motion Sensor watches traffic to and from darknets, which are routable prefixes that have no end hosts attached, and to unassigned and unannounced address space. By watching this activity one can understand and detect scanning activity, DDoS worms, worm infected hosts and misconfigured hosts. At the time of writing it monitored approximately 17 million prefixes, about 1.2 percent of the IPv4 address space, and it highlighted two characteristics of attacks: malicious attacks are more targeted than one might assume, and a vulnerability in a system does not necessarily lead to a threat to that system, because it may not be exploited if the perceived benefit to the attacker looks small. Data from the sensor and other sources indicates that attackers increasingly use information from social networking sites to target their attacks and pick perceived easy targets, such as computers running very old versions of systems or new unpatched vulnerabilities. This form of passive collection is also known as a network telescope. BCP 38 still had not been widely deployed, perhaps because of the incentive issue, and BCP 84 extends it to multihomed networks. Deep packet inspection at high speed across layers 2 to 7 was being developed by several vendors, and the workshop suggested that operators and standards bodies cooperate on "How To" documents for configuring networks. Methods such as SHRED, which aims to make it increasingly expensive for spammers to use email while normal users keep the service they expect, were discussed without agreement on their effectiveness.

The "Aladdin's Lamp" session collected wishes rather than conclusions. Operators wanted a reliable point of contact in each administrative domain for security coordination, since the whois database of registration details for IP addresses and autonomous system numbers, and the common mailbox names established for certain roles and services, are largely unused, partly because unwanted traffic itself makes them unusable. They wanted organised security testing: new hardware and software is tested extensively for performance, but almost not at all for security, and a shared test bed for such testing would help. They wanted equipment and software to come with a simple and effective default setting for security, and an automated mechanism for sharing information about attacks, vulnerabilities and threat sources. They wanted automatic filtering of unwanted traffic, though the filtering of spam, viruses and malware sent by email is already practicable but imperfect because it relies on heuristics and is part of an arms race with spammers trying to evade the filters. And they wanted the spam problem fixed, since a large fraction of the email traffic coming into enterprises today is spam.
sections.plainLanguage: Things in the pipeline include shared policy repositories, flow-based tools that learn what normal traffic looks like so they can spot what is not, and sensors that watch unused address space. The wishes are practical: a working contact point for every network, security testing of new equipment, secure defaults, and a way to share information about attacks.

sections.title: What the Workshop Recommended
sections.content:
The workshop spent its last two hours on what engineering and research work the IETF and the IRTF could pursue and what actions the IAB could take. The hard questions it raised were about the role of cryptographic mechanisms in the overall Internet architecture, whether to harden the shell or rely on deep packet inspection to filter out bad traffic; about how far the community is willing to go in curtailing the openness of the Internet and increasing system complexity, and which architectural principles to preserve on the way; about whether the core routing infrastructure, the ideal target of minimal cost and maximal disruption, really needs an unlinked and separately managed control plane to be secure; and about whether the economic substructure can be changed, for which a further workshop was suggested.

For the medium or long term the workshop suggested tightening the security of the core routing infrastructure, cleaning up the Internet Routing Registry and securing both the database and the access to it so that it can be used for routing verifications, taking down botnets, developing effective measures to reduce unwanted traffic to a tiny fraction of its current volume and keep it under control, and community education so that people use the updated host, router and ingress filtering best current practices.

The immediately actionable steps were for the IETF to update the host requirements, developed in 1989 and overdue after the fundamental changes the Internet has been through since, to update the router requirements, developed in 1995 and equally overdue, and to update the ingress filtering recommendations BCP 38 and BCP 84. The IAB was asked to inform the community about the existence of the underground economy, and the IRTF was asked to study the underground economy further and start research on developing effective countermeasures. Overall, the attendees wanted to raise the community's awareness of the underground economy and to have the community as a whole undertake a systematic examination of the current situation and develop both near-term and long-term plans.
sections.plainLanguage: The recommendations are mostly unglamorous: update the host and router requirement documents, update the address filtering rules, tell the world about the underground economy, and study it properly. The bigger questions, about cryptography, openness and money, were left open for another workshop.

viz.caption: WHY THERE IS NO EFFECTIVE DETERRENCE

items.title: Money
items.text: Big economic incentives and a rich environment to exploit.

items.title: Responsibility
items.text: No specific party carries responsibility for resolving the problem.

items.title: Traceability
items.text: No auditing system to trace attacks back to their sources.

items.title: Law
items.text: No well established legal regulations to punish offenders.
